case_brief.incident_description: Naledi had worked for the agency for three years. She told her manager that she was pregnant and two weeks later was informed that her role was redundant. She says the business had recently won two new clients, that another junior employee in the same team was retained, and that she received no written section 189(3) notice or meaningful consultation before the decision. She was offered one month notice and severance. The employer described the decision as restructuring.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: I told my manager I was pregnant and two weeks later they retrenched me. We had just won two new clients. The junior in my team stayed and nobody consulted with me before telling me my job was gone.
case_brief.recommended_next_step: Urgent WP letter challenging the retrenchment process and raising the pregnancy-linked dismissal risk.
weaknesses: Employer may produce financial or restructuring evidence not yet seen

letter:
Background

1. We act on the instructions of our client, Ms Naledi Dlamini, in respect of the termination of her employment with Orbit Creative Agency (Pty) Ltd. We are instructed to address this correspondence to the Managing Director. All further correspondence in this matter should be directed to our offices and not to our client directly.

2. This letter is written on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis for the purpose of exploring a negotiated resolution of our client's claims. Nothing in this letter constitutes an admission of fact or law by our client, and all of our client's rights are expressly reserved to pursue the appropriate statutory remedies, including referral to the CCMA, without further notice should a resolution not be reached.

3. Our client was employed by Orbit Creative Agency (Pty) Ltd for a period of approximately three years. To the extent that length of service is not otherwise confirmed in documentation available to us, we record this on the basis of our client's own account.

4. In or around late October 2026, our client disclosed to her manager that she was pregnant. To the extent that the precise date of that disclosure, as opposed to the date on which she was subsequently notified of the redundancy decision, remains to be confirmed between the parties, we record the sequence on the basis of our client's own account and invite the employer's confirmation. Approximately two weeks after that disclosure, our client was informed that her role had been identified as redundant and that her employment would accordingly be terminated on grounds described by the employer as restructuring.

5. Our client was offered one month's notice and a severance payment. She was not issued with any written notice in terms of section 189(3) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 prior to the decision to terminate her employment, and no process of meaningful consultation preceded that decision.

6. Our client reports that the agency had, shortly before her dismissal, secured two new client accounts, a development that she understood to indicate an expanding rather than a contracting operational need. We invite the employer's confirmation or response on this point.

7. Turning to a standalone point of comparison, our client reports that another junior employee within her own team was retained notwithstanding the stated restructuring rationale. To the extent that this is confirmed, our client's position is that she and the retained junior employee occupied materially similar roles, and that the only material point of difference between them at the relevant time was our client's recent disclosure of her pregnancy. We invite the employer to address this directly.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: operational requirements under section 188(1) read with the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025: The fairness of a dismissal is assessed under section 188(1) of the LRA, which requires both a fair reason and a fair procedure. Where an employer relies on operational requirements, the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (which has replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 and governs the current analysis) applies at paragraphs 22 to 24, read with section 189 of the LRA. On the facts available to us, our client was not issued with any written notice under section 189(3) setting out the reasons for the proposed retrenchment, the alternatives considered, the proposed selection criteria or severance terms, and no meaningful consultation process preceded the decision. A process confined to a single announcement of redundancy, without prior consultation or disclosure of the matters required under section 189(3), does not meet the standard required for a fair retrenchment. This is compounded by our client's account that the agency had recently secured two new client accounts, which sits uneasily with a stated rationale of contracting operational need, and by the retention of a comparator junior employee in the same team. Taken together, these matters raise a serious question as to whether the operational requirement advanced was genuine, and as to whether the selection of our client for redundancy was fair and objectively justified.

2. Automatically unfair dismissal: pregnancy under section 187(1)(e) of the LRA and the EEA pregnancy protections: Section 187(1)(e) of the LRA renders a dismissal automatically unfair where the reason for the dismissal is the employee's pregnancy or any reason related to her pregnancy. The Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 affords corresponding protection against unfair treatment on the grounds of pregnancy. On our client's account, she disclosed her pregnancy to her manager, and within approximately two weeks was informed that her role was redundant. That temporal proximity is, in itself, a material fact calling for explanation. It is reinforced by two further matters: the agency's recent acquisition of two new client accounts, which undermines the stated operational rationale for redundancy, and the retention of a comparator junior employee in the same team whose only apparent point of difference from our client was the recent pregnancy disclosure. Viewed cumulatively, these facts support a reasonable inference of a causal connection between the pregnancy disclosure and the decision to terminate our client's employment, which our client is entitled to have tested. Should that causal connection be established, the dismissal would be automatically unfair under section 187(1)(e), attracting the enhanced compensation ceiling under section 194(3) of the LRA rather than the ordinary section 194(1) cap.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without derogating from any of the above, and in the interests of a pragmatic and commercially sensible resolution, our client proposes the following terms of settlement:

• Ex gratia compensation on a total cost to company basis, calibrated to reflect the litigation risk arising from the procedural and substantive defects identified above and, given the automatically unfair dismissal overlay, having regard to the compensation framework of up to 24 months' remuneration under section 194(3) of the LRA (alternatively up to 12 months' remuneration under section 194(1)), to be agreed as a single figure.

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Payment of accrued but untaken leave pay owed under section 40 of the BCEA.

• Confirmation that provident or pension fund contributions, where applicable, are paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the fund.

• Confirmation that UIF contributions are paid up to date and provision of a completed UI-19 certificate.

• A certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA.

• An agreed reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties.

• An undertaking by the employer and its representatives not to disparage our client in any communication, reference or representation to any third party.

• Confidentiality as to the terms of settlement, the negotiations and the existence of the dispute, as between the parties and their respective advisers.

• That the terms of settlement be reduced to a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved pending such signature.

Our client's exposure assessment reflects the combination of the apparent absence of a fair process under section 189 and the serious question raised as to a causal connection with her pregnancy disclosure under section 187(1)(e). Should these matters proceed to referral and arbitration or adjudication, our client would be entitled to pursue compensation of up to 24 months' remuneration under section 194(3) of the LRA, in addition to the statutory entitlements referred to above. We consider that a negotiated resolution at this stage is in the interests of both parties and avoids the cost, delay and reputational exposure of contested proceedings.

We invite a substantive response to this letter within 7 calendar days of the date of this letter, failing which our client's instructions are to proceed with referral of this dispute to the CCMA without further notice.

All of our client's rights are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: Minor over-precision: 'late October 2026' is asserted for the pregnancy disclosure when the brief only gives a single incident_date (2026-10-30) which appears to attach to the dismissal/redundancy notification event, not the disclosure. The draft does flag this with conditional wording but still anchors a specific timeframe ('late October 2026') to the disclosure event rather than to the confirmed redundancy notification date, which is a date-to-event attribution risk given the brief's single generic incident_date.
criteria.required_fix: Attach the confirmed incident_date to the event it most plausibly supports (the redundancy notification) and describe the disclosure date only as preceding it by approximately two weeks, without assigning a specific month/year label to the disclosure itself unless the brief supports it.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'In or around late October 2026, our client disclosed to her manager that she was pregnant... To the extent that the precise date of that disclosure... remains to be confirmed...'

criteria.problem: Generally strong and proportionate; correctly reflects HIGH merit band, s189 and s187(1)(e) overlay, cap-relative framing, and ties facts (no notice, no consultation, new clients, comparator retention, timing) to both claims. However the operational requirements claim is titled/framed under section 188(1) general unfair dismissal language blended with section 189 retrenchment analysis without first anchoring squarely in section 189 as the primary framework, which slightly muddies the correct track-specific statutory anchor for a retrenchment case (section 189/189A is the governing provision, with section 188(1) as the overarching fairness requirement).
criteria.required_fix: Lead the retrenchment claim with section 189 (and the Code paragraphs applicable to operational requirements) as the primary anchor, with section 188(1) referenced as the overarching fairness requirement, to keep the statutory hierarchy clear for a retrenchment-track matter.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Claim 1 title: 'Unfair dismissal: operational requirements under section 188(1) read with the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' and body opens with section 188(1) before turning to section 189
Tone throughout is controlled, factual-before-argumentative, uses 'Our client's position is', 'we invite', 'without further notice', avoiding bluster or stock aggressive phrases.

criteria.problem: The claims are distinct and well-headed, but the comparator paragraph is introduced in the narrative with 'Turning to a standalone point of comparison,' which is good practice, yet the factual background paragraphs could more clearly separate background/chronology from the legal-analysis signposting already embedded in paragraph 6-7; minor stylistic overlap but not a duplication issue.
criteria.required_fix: Keep the comparator paragraph strictly factual (the comparator's role and retention) and reserve the inferential 'sole material difference' argument for the legal claims section to maintain a cleaner facts-to-law progression.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Paragraph 7 begins analysis-like framing ('our client's position is that she and the retained junior employee occupied materially similar roles') inside what is nominally a factual background paragraph.

criteria.problem: Clear and proportionate; response window correctly capped at 7 calendar days; settlement clauses follow standing order substantially. Minor: the ex gratia clause uses 'to be agreed as a single figure' which is acceptable but could be tightened; non-disparagement is correctly one-way against the employer only.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'We invite a substantive response to this letter within 7 calendar days...'; 'An undertaking by the employer and its representatives not to disparage our client...'

criteria.problem: The Code citation in claim 1 contains an internally confusing parenthetical: 'the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (which has replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 and governs the current analysis)' - this appears to be a drafting/copy error where the 'former' instrument name is identical to the 'current' one, creating a nonsensical self-referential statement that should name the actual predecessor (Schedule 8) or simply omit the parenthetical. While it avoids the literal word 'Schedule 8', the garbled formulation is a safety/accuracy defect requiring correction. No Schedule 8 reference, no case law, no salary figures, no duplicate salutation/closing, and BCEA s37/s38 notice-pay formulation is fully compliant with the permitted pattern.
criteria.required_fix: Correct the parenthetical to either remove it entirely or state accurately that the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 is the current governing instrument, without implying it replaced an identically named instrument.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (which has replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 and governs the current analysis) applies at paragraphs 22 to 24'

initial_assessment.supervisory_summary: The submitted Part A content consists only of well-drafted, factually faithful opening and background paragraphs that correctly follow the instruction/capacity, purpose and background order and use proper conditional wording for unconfirmed facts. However, for a HIGH merit-band, FULL WP letter the draft omits the entire legal analysis, settlement preamble, settlement clauses, exposure paragraph, response window and reservation of rights required by section 3A.1 of the Employee WP skill.
